criteria.name: visual_grounding
criteria.description: Visual grounding requires that every claim in the answer must be directly, unambiguously supported by visible elements in the image — including objects, their spatial relationships, attributes (color, shape, texture, position, state), actions, and presence/absence — with no hallucination, omission, or inference unsupported by visual evidence. Annotators must: (1) verify that each stated visual element is verifiable from the image — if an element is not visible, it must be explicitly marked as absent or uncertain; (2) penalize hallucinations (inventing non-visible objects, states, or labels) — including misidentifications of visible elements — but not misinterpretations of visible content (e.g., calling a ‘L-shaped couch’ a ‘U-shaped sofa’ if the visual structure is L-shaped); (3) penalize omissions of clearly visible, semantically relevant elements (e.g., omitting a visible label like ‘Questions’ when it is contextually significant); (4) accept contextually plausible interpretations (e.g., ‘arrogant’ based on facial expression, ‘warehouse’ based on shelves) if visually supported — but never penalize for subjective or aesthetic interpretations (e.g., ‘playful’, ‘messy’) if grounded in visible structure; (5) signal uncertainty explicitly when visual evidence is ambiguous (e.g., motion blur, occlusion, low resolution) — not assume or invent states; (6) treat visible text, logos, or labels as integral visual content — misrepresenting or ignoring them is a violation; (7) allow descriptive granularity and artistic interpretation (e.g., ‘curved’, ‘L-shaped’, ‘icy’) if grounded in visual cues — even if non-literal or stylized — but penalize if it fabricates non-existent forms (e.g., ‘geometric’ without visible regular shapes); (8) distinguish between semantic misidentification (e.g., ‘driven’ vs. ‘riding’) and hallucination — penalize only if the misidentification contradicts visible evidence; (9) evaluate presence/absence claims based on visual evidence — not by omission or assumption; (10) apply only to visual content — not to inference, abstract truth, emotion, or opinion — and mark such cases as inapplicable. Visual grounding is not about literalism, but about visual fidelity — it rewards accurate descriptions even if they are compositional or non-literal, as long as they reflect what is visually present. Accuracy is measured by strict visual alignment — not by linguistic polish, contextual plausibility, or stylistic elegance — and is only applicable when the question asks for visual content. If an answer is factually incorrect or hallucinated, it is automatically invalid for grounding — regardless of visual detail or confidence. The criterion does not penalize for including non-essential or background visual elements — as long as they are visible and not hallucinated. If visual evidence is insufficient (e.g., ambiguous color, partially occluded object), the answer must express uncertainty — not assert a specific detail. Visual grounding is not applicable when the question asks for inference, abstract truth, or non-visual content — in which case, the focus should be on factual consistency or plausibility. When in doubt, prioritize visual truth over stylistic or interpretive flair — and never penalize for contextually plausible interpretations if they are visually grounded. Workers must treat ‘inapplicable’ cases with care — only when the question is clearly about inference, opinion, or non-visual content. Finally, if the question asks for count, the answer must reflect the visually verifiable count — even when uncertain — uncertainty is only appropriate for ambiguity, not for miscounting. The criterion applies only to claims that are visually verifiable — not to claims that are factually correct in the real world but not visible. Hallucinations include both omission and incorrect quantification — miscounting is a hallucination. Descriptions of object composition (e.g., ‘L-shaped couch’) are acceptable if visually supported — even if the object appears as multiple segments. Mislabeling abstract visual elements (e.g., ‘lines’ vs. ‘shapes’) is not a hallucination unless it contradicts visible structure. Contextually reasonable aesthetic or interpretive language (e.g., ‘scenic beauty’, ‘contrasting’) is allowed if grounded in visual structure — but only if it does not fabricate non-visible details. The criterion does not penalize for including visible text or labels — even if they are not explicitly asked for — as long as they are accurately described. Visual grounding is not applicable to non-visual descriptions — e.g., ‘politician’ — which are inferred or semantic — and should be marked as inapplicable. The goal is faithful representation of the image — not exhaustive listing — and any claim that misrepresents visible content is a hallucination, regardless of plausibility. Workers must avoid conflating omission with hallucination — if an object is not visible, it must be explicitly stated as absent or uncertain — not assumed to be present. Descriptions must accurately reflect visible text and labels — e.g., ‘Answers’ vs. ‘Questions’ — misidentifying visible labels is a hallucination. If the image supports multiple plausible interpretations, the answer that aligns most closely with the literal structure or most clearly supported by visual cues should be favored — not the one that is ‘more explicit’ or ‘more specific’ if it misrepresents the visual setup. Finally, if an answer includes a term that is not visually present or not contextually appropriate to the visual content, it should be penalized — even if it is factually correct in general knowledge. The criterion does not apply to aesthetic, emotional, or interpretive judgments — these are evaluated under semantic_coherence_with_image_context. The criterion is inapplicable when the question asks for non-visual metadata (e.g., titles, artist names) or semantic inferences (e.g., role, intent) — and must be marked as inapplicable in such cases. Hallucinations are defined as any claim that invents or misrepresents non-visible visual elements — not as claims that are factually wrong about visible elements (e.g., misinterpreting relative size or position — if visually verifiable, it is not a hallucination).

criteria.name: factual_consistency
criteria.description: An answer is factually consistent if and only if every claim about visual elements — including object identity, attributes, positions, states, counts, or relationships — directly matches what is visually verifiable in the image, with strict adherence to literal visual evidence. Annotators must: (1) verify each visual claim against the image at a granular level (using zoom or close inspection if needed), penalizing only claims that are definitively contradicted or hallucinated — not claims that are visually ambiguous or artistically stylized; (2) treat 'absence' as a valid claim only if the element is visibly absent (e.g., a car is not visible in a small portion of the image), and penalize claims of presence for absent elements; (3) penalize hallucinations (invented visual elements not present) and misidentifications (e.g., calling a rug a bear) as factual inconsistencies — even if minor or plausible — but not omissions of non-essential or ambiguous details; (4) allow proportional or relative descriptions (e.g., 'small portion', 'most of the space') as long as they are visually plausible and do not contradict observable proportions or identities; (5) allow contextually grounded inferences (e.g., 'warehouse' from shelves, 'indoor' from lighting) as long as they are visually supported — not penalized if plausible and inferred from visual cues — but penalize inferred actions or system attributes (e.g., 'browsing') unless explicitly marked as uncertain; (6) penalize only visual contradictions — not subjective emotional or behavioral interpretations (e.g., 'angry', 'happy', 'arrogant') — which are allowed if grounded in visible cues (e.g., facial expression, posture); (7) if both answers are factually inconsistent, neither should be favored — mark as inapplicable or both as equally bad — and do not select one over another based on plausibility or style; (8) if only one answer is factually consistent, it should be preferred — factual consistency is not a binary filter for the entire answer but a claim-by-claim evaluation; (9) if visual evidence is too ambiguous to verify any claim with certainty, mark the criterion as inapplicable — do not penalize for omission or ambiguity unless it creates a contradiction; (10) do not penalize for colloquial or aesthetic interpretations (e.g., 'water scooters' for jet skis, 'scenic beauty') as long as they are visually grounded — factual inconsistency applies only to literal misrepresentations; (11) if the question is non-visual (e.g., abstract, hypothetical, or theoretical), the criterion is inapplicable — evaluate only visual claims; (12) numerical claims (e.g., counts, object instances) must be verified with precision — undercounting is penalized if the image shows more; (13) misinterpretations of visible elements (e.g., misidentifying color or shape) are factual inconsistencies — not hallucinations — and must be penalized even if they appear plausible; (14) omission of a visually present element (especially if the question explicitly asks for it) is a factual inconsistency — penalize only if it contradicts the question’s scope or intent; (15) if both answers are factually consistent, prefer the one with higher visual precision or completeness — but do not penalize one for being less literal or less absolute — evaluate under other criteria; (16) the criterion applies only to visual claims — not to abstract inferences, emotional states, or contextual interpretations — which are evaluated under other criteria (e.g., visual_cue_alignment, cultural_or_situational_appropriateness).

criteria.name: completeness
criteria.description: Completeness evaluates whether a factually correct and visually grounded answer includes all visual elements that are explicitly or implicitly required by the question’s scope — i.e., elements that are both visually present and necessary to fully answer the question. This criterion applies ONLY when: (1) the answer is factually consistent (verified under factual_consistency first), and (2) the question explicitly or implicitly requests multiple visual aspects, attributes, or a list (e.g., ‘describe X and Y’, ‘list all foreground objects’, ‘what is the color and position of the object?’). It is inapplicable for: (a) simple yes/no, presence/absence, or general description questions (e.g., ‘What is in the image?’), (b) questions that do not request multiple visual aspects, and (c) any answer that is factually incorrect, hallucinated, or misidentified — such answers are disqualified under factual_consistency and cannot be evaluated under completeness. An answer is incomplete if it omits a visually present element that is explicitly required by the question’s scope — e.g., omitting the collar color when asked ‘What color is the cat’s collar?’. Completeness does NOT penalize: (1) omission of non-essential or irrelevant visual elements (e.g., background objects, decorative items, non-core context), (2) inclusion of non-requested but visually present details (e.g., a table in a scene about posture), or (3) descriptive precision that is factually accurate and visually grounded (e.g., ‘legs bent’ vs. ‘legs straight’ — even if less specific). Completeness does NOT apply to: (a) functional, semantic, or contextual interpretations (e.g., ‘sandwich’ or ‘warehouse’) unless explicitly tied to requested visual attributes, (b) inferred states or actions unless visually supported, or (c) aesthetic or evaluative language (e.g., ‘beautiful’, ‘playful’) — those are evaluated under semantic_coherence_with_image_context. Annotators must: (1) verify factual_consistency first — if an answer is factually incorrect, completeness is inapplicable and the answer is disqualified, (2) evaluate completeness only in the context of the question’s explicit scope — not as an absolute measure of ‘covering everything’, (3) penalize only when a required visual element is omitted — not when an element is included but not requested, (4) reward descriptive specificity that is factually correct — even if unusual or stylistic — as long as it is visually grounded, (5) treat ‘visually present’ as clearly observable — not inferred, contextually implied, or abstractly suggested — and (6) mark the criterion as inapplicable if the question does not request multiple aspects or specific attributes. Completeness is not a tiebreaker for factual errors — if one answer is factually correct and the other is not, the correct answer is preferred by default, regardless of completeness. When visual evidence is ambiguous, uncertainty should be signaled — not assumed or invented — to avoid penalizing for omission. Completeness does not override factual_consistency — if an answer is factually incorrect, it is disqualified regardless of how complete it appears. The goal is to ensure that all required visual elements are included — not to force exhaustive coverage, abstraction, or stylistic detail — and to avoid penalizing for omission of non-essential or irrelevant details. Completeness is evaluated only for factually correct answers — and annotators must mark it as inapplicable for any answer that is factually incorrect, hallucinated, or misidentified. If both answers are factually correct, preference should be determined by other criteria — not by completeness — and completeness should never be used to resolve ties or override factual errors.

criteria.name: calibrated_uncertainty
criteria.description: Evaluates whether the answer appropriately signals uncertainty when visual evidence is ambiguous — using phrases like 'likely', 'possibly', or 'based on what I see' — without over- or under-stating confidence. Applicable only when the visual evidence is ambiguous or insufficient to support absolute certainty. Accuracy is measured by whether the degree of uncertainty matches the visual ambiguity — not by linguistic style or completeness. This criterion is inapplicable for clearly verifiable or hallucinated claims. Annotators must penalize claims that assert certainty without visual support, and reward cautious phrasing when ambiguity is present.

criteria.name: accuracy_of_positioning
criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer correctly describes the spatial relationship between two or more distinct, visually identifiable objects — specifically their relative position, proximity, orientation, or compositional arrangement — based solely on visually verifiable cues (occlusion, depth, perspective, shadows, frame placement). It applies ONLY when the question explicitly requests spatial positioning (e.g., 'where is X relative to Y?', 'which object is in front of?', 'arranged how?'). Annotators must: (1) FIRST verify object identity is visually grounded — if an object is misidentified or hallucinated, the spatial claim is invalid and the criterion is marked 'inapplicable'; (2) evaluate positioning claims using ONLY visual evidence — no inference, narrative, or contextual plausibility allowed (e.g., 'hanging from the ceiling' requires visible attachment; 'facing' requires visible orientation); (3) accept vague or indirect descriptors ('near', 'in front of') if visually supported — but penalize hallucinated positions (e.g., 'door behind table' if no door exists); (4) prioritize visual fidelity over linguistic specificity — even verbose or descriptive answers are correct if visually accurate; (5) if spatial relationships are ambiguous, prefer conservative, literal descriptions — penalize speculative inferences (e.g., 'likely part of room structure') — but do not omit spatial claims unless the question does not request them; (6) if the answer is factually inconsistent (e.g., misidentifies or hallucinates an object), it is disqualified — mark the criterion as 'inapplicable' and evaluate preference using other criteria (factual_consistency, visual_grounding, completeness); (7) if the question does not request spatial positioning, the criterion is 'inapplicable' — even if the answer contains spatial language — and preference must be determined using other criteria; (8) spatial relationships must be grounded in visible mounting or structural form — inferred or hallucinated attachment invalidates the claim; (9) if the question asks for spatial positioning, the answer must include explicit directional or positional cues — vague terms like 'talking to' without directional context are insufficient; (10) non-spatial inferences (e.g., activity, intent, motion) are outside scope — evaluated under other criteria; (11) accuracy is binary — the description must be visually verifiable and grounded, or it is incorrect — no partial credit; (12) DO NOT penalize for including additional, verifiable spatial relationships or objects — even if not explicitly requested — as long as they are factually correct and visually present; (13) DO NOT penalize for being more detailed or comprehensive — if the additional details are visually accurate and grounded — the goal is to reward visual fidelity, not minimalism; (14) DO NOT penalize for descriptive terms like 'messy', 'unstructured', or 'irregular' — if visually supported — these are valid descriptors and not hallucinations; (15) DO NOT penalize for omitting objects irrelevant to the question’s scope — e.g., background objects like doors may be omitted if the question does not ask for structural relationships; (16) DO NOT penalize for contextually grounded inferences — e.g., 'attending to her hair' is valid if visually supported by posture and hand position — even if it involves object positioning; (17) DO NOT evaluate spatial accuracy for misidentified objects — if object identity is wrong, mark criterion as 'inapplicable' — spatial claims are irrelevant without correct object grounding; (18) DO NOT use this criterion to resolve factual errors — if an answer is factually wrong, preference must be determined by factual_consistency, not spatial accuracy; (19) DO NOT use this criterion as a tiebreaker — if both answers are factually consistent, spatial accuracy may be used to break ties — but only if the question explicitly requests spatial positioning; (20) DO NOT penalize for omitting spatial claims unless the question explicitly requests them — and do not assume spatial positioning is required based on verbosity or perceived precision — only the question’s explicit scope matters. This criterion does NOT apply to: (a) object presence/absence, (b) object identity, (c) non-spatial attributes (color, material, texture), (d) inferred states (open, broken, wet), (e) motion or activity (driving, running), or (f) abstract or aesthetic commentary — all evaluated under other criteria. If both answers are factually consistent, the one with better spatial accuracy wins — but if one is factually wrong, it cannot be favored, even if spatially accurate.

criteria.name: accuracy_of_attributes
criteria.description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly describes intrinsic visual properties of objects — including color, texture, shape, size, material, posture, orientation, and implied visual structure — as directly observable in the image. Applicable only when the question asks for or implies such attributes. Not applicable if the object is misidentified, not visually present, or if the question does not request visual attributes. Penalize hallucinations (e.g., describing a ‘tie’ on a shirt when none is visible) or misinterpretations (e.g., calling a curved track ‘straight’). Reward precise, visually grounded descriptions even if they include nuanced terms like ‘semi-dark’ or ‘slightly bent’. Ignore subjective interpretations (e.g., ‘arrogant’) or contextual inferences (e.g., ‘in a warehouse’). Attribute accuracy is not evaluated if the object’s identity is ambiguous or if the attribute is unverifiable due to image quality or perspective. If the answer correctly identifies the object and its visual properties, even if the object is not fully visible, it is considered accurate. Attribute descriptions must be tied to correctly identified objects — misidentification invalidates attribute accuracy. Do not penalize for omitting non-existent attributes or for describing absence (e.g., ‘no question mark’). Avoid applying this criterion to spatial relationships, actions, or inferred states — those fall under other criteria like visual grounding or visual cue alignment. Prefer descriptions that are factually faithful to the image over vague or metaphorical labels (e.g., ‘silhouette of a person’ is acceptable, ‘icon’ is not). Allow for ‘inapplicable’ when the attribute is ambiguous or not visually verifiable. Accuracy is judged solely on visual fidelity — not on stylistic preference, added flair, or conceptual interpretation.

criteria.name: biological_or_contextual_plausibility
criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer’s interpretation of visual content aligns with known real-world biological or contextual behaviors — but only when the answer involves living entities (animals, humans) or real-world physical interactions (e.g., movement, object use, spatial relationships). It does NOT apply to: (1) visual attributes (color, shape, text), (2) static object counts or enumeration, (3) abstract or symbolic imagery (logos, icons), (4) spatial positioning (evaluated under visual_grounding or accuracy_of_positioning), or (5) hallucinations or unsupported inferences. When applicable, annotators should: (a) confirm the answer’s claims are grounded in visual evidence, (b) assess whether the described behavior or context is biologically or physically plausible in the real world (e.g., a zebra can’t fly), (c) avoid penalizing for non-standard but visually grounded interpretations (e.g., a person holding a phone while sitting), and (d) prioritize visual fidelity over plausibility if there is a contradiction. This criterion should never override factual_consistency or hallucination avoidance. If the visual evidence is ambiguous, the answer should reflect uncertainty, not fabricate a plausible scenario. Examples: 'A dog running toward a ball is plausible'; 'A person flying without wings is implausible'; 'A cake with frosting is plausible (even if unusual)'; 'The color of the shirt is red — not a plausibility judgment'.

criteria.name: consistency_within_answer
criteria.description: Is the answer internally consistent? Annotators prefer answers that do not contradict themselves (e.g., describing a person as both holding glasses and holding their head, when only one action is visible).

criteria.name: visual_detail_preservation
criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer preserves only visually verifiable, factually accurate, and contextually relevant visual details — not speculative, hallucinated, or unsupported elements. Annotators should reward answers that include precise, observable attributes (e.g., color, texture, spatial relationships, object identity, count, or brand text) that are clearly present in the image, even if described informally. The criterion is inapplicable if the question does not require granular visual description (e.g., ‘What is happening?’), or if the visual evidence is too ambiguous to support any specific detail — in which case, the criterion should be marked as inapplicable, not penalized. Accuracy is prioritized over quantity: any hallucinated detail (invented or misattributed object/attribute not visible) invalidates the answer, regardless of its apparent relevance or detail level. Omission of non-critical, non-hallucinated details (e.g., undershirts, background elements) is acceptable if irrelevant or visually ambiguous. Annotators must verify each claimed detail against the image: if a detail is visually present and accurate, it is preserved; if it is not present or misidentified, it is a hallucination and penalized. Contextual or inferential details (e.g., ‘this suggests a dining area’) are acceptable if grounded in visual cues (e.g., chairs, table, utensils) and not invented. The criterion does not penalize slight imprecision in color or texture if still visually grounded (e.g., ‘green’ vs ‘blue’ for turquoise). Visual metaphors, stylized forms (e.g., ‘bent legs’ for a statue), or implied motion are acceptable if visually implied or present — not if invented. The goal is visual fidelity, not linguistic polish or completeness. If both answers contain hallucinations, the one closer to visual truth should be preferred; if neither is correct, mark as inapplicable. This criterion is only applied when the question explicitly requires visual granularity — e.g., ‘describe the object’s color and position’, ‘count the windows’, or ‘identify the texture’. It does not apply to high-level scene descriptions, abstract inferences, or emotional interpretations.

criteria.name: object_boundary_accuracy
criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer accurately describes the physical, spatial, or structural boundaries of visually identifiable objects — including edge definition, occlusion, fragmentation, and spatial containment — without misrepresenting or merging distinct visual entities. It applies ONLY when the question explicitly requests object shape, spatial limits, occlusion, or structural integrity (e.g., 'describe the shape', 'is the object fragmented?', 'what is the occlusion relationship?'). It is inapplicable for: (1) object presence/absence (evaluated under visual_grounding), (2) object identity or labeling (evaluated under visual_grounding or factual_consistency), (3) color, texture, or material (evaluated under accuracy_of_attributes), (4) spatial positioning or motion (evaluated under accuracy_of_positioning or temporal_consistency), (5) inferred states or behavior (evaluated under plausibility_of_inferred_states), (6) semantic interpretations (evaluated under semantic_coherence_with_image_context or avoidance_of_overinterpretation), (7) text or label descriptions (evaluated under visual_grounding), (8) aesthetic or stylistic interpretations (evaluated under semantic_coherence_with_image_context), (9) general arrangement or compositional structure (evaluated under multi_object_relationship_accuracy or visual_cue_alignment), and (10) questions that do not request boundary-related details. Annotators must: (a) verify that the question explicitly asks for shape, occlusion, fragmentation, or spatial containment — if not, mark the criterion as 'inapplicable'; (b) evaluate only the visual structure of objects — not their identity, label, or semantic role — and ensure boundaries are grounded in visible edges, occlusions, or containment; (c) penalize only when the answer misrepresents visible boundaries — e.g., describing a fragmented object as intact, or merging distinct entities as one — but not when it accurately describes boundaries (e.g., 'partially occluded', 'fragmented', 'collapsed'); (d) reward accurate boundary descriptions — even if less detailed — as long as they reflect visual evidence; (e) never penalize for descriptive precision — only for misrepresentation; (f) not penalize for including non-essential or non-requested background details — as long as they do not misrepresent object boundaries; (g) not penalize for omitting non-requested visual elements — if they are not critical to the question’s scope; (h) not penalize for using descriptive or inferential language — as long as it does not misrepresent boundaries; (i) not penalize for stylistic or aesthetic language — as long as it does not misrepresent boundaries; (j) not penalize for contextually grounded interpretations — as long as they do not misrepresent visible boundaries; (k) not penalize for describing objects as 'packaging box' or 'box' — even if visually fragmented — as long as it is not misrepresenting the object’s physical limits; (l) not penalize for describing non-geometric shapes — as long as they are visually verifiable; (m) not penalize for describing abstract visual forms — as long as they are visually verifiable; (n) not penalize for describing non-visual or hallucinated claims — as long as they are not misrepresenting visible boundaries; (o) not penalize for describing logos or icons — as long as they are visually verifiable; (p) not penalize for describing non-literal or metaphorical forms — as long as they are visually verifiable; (q) not penalize for describing non-physical or non-spatial boundaries — as long as they are visually verifiable; (r) not penalize for describing non-visible boundaries — as long as they are not hallucinated; (s) not penalize for describing boundaries that are not explicitly requested — as long as they are not hallucinated or misrepresenting visible boundaries; (t) not penalize for describing boundaries that are not explicitly requested — as long as they are not hallucinated or misrepresenting visible boundaries; (u) not penalize for describing boundaries that are not explicitly requested — as long as they are not hallucinated or misrepresenting visible boundaries; (v) not penalize for describing boundaries that are not explicitly requested — as long as they are not hallucinated or misrepresenting visible boundaries; (w) not penalize for describing boundaries that are not explicitly requested — as long as they are not hallucinated or misrepresenting visible boundaries; (x) not penalize for describing boundaries that are not explicitly requested — as long as they are not hallucinated or misrepresenting visible boundaries; (y) not penalize for describing boundaries that are not explicitly requested — as long as they are not hallucinated or misrepresenting visible boundaries; (z) not penalize for describing boundaries that are not explicitly requested — as long as they are not hallucinated or misrepresenting visible boundaries. Accuracy is binary: the boundary description must be visually verifiable and accurate — or it is incorrect. The criterion is designed to ensure visual fidelity of object limits — not to reward stylistic detail, narrative plausibility, or semantic coherence — and must never be used to resolve factual errors or override visual_grounding. If the answer is factually incorrect or hallucinated, it is disqualified under factual_consistency — and this criterion is not invoked. The goal is to reward accurate descriptions of physical, spatial, or structural limits — not to penalize for descriptive imprecision, stylistic choices, or contextual inferences — as long as they do not misrepresent visible boundaries.

criteria.name: visual_cue_alignment
criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer correctly interprets and uses observable visual cues (e.g., posture, gaze direction, facial expression, object orientation, body positioning) to support a reasonable inference of emotion, intent, or action — not to describe observable facts directly. Annotators should only apply this criterion when the question explicitly asks for interpretation of emotion, intent, or implied action, and when such cues are clearly visible in the image. The answer must be factually consistent with the image and cannot rely on hallucinated cues. Misusing visual cues to justify false claims (e.g., claiming a horse is leaning to infer a curved track when none is visible) is penalized. The criterion is inapplicable if: (1) the question asks for factual description (e.g., 'what is in the image?'), (2) no interpretable visual cues are present, or (3) the answer provides no inference based on cues. Accuracy is judged by whether the inferred claim is both grounded in verifiable visual cues and contextually plausible — not by how 'creative' or 'detailed' the interpretation is. Workers must defer to factual consistency if visual cues conflict with it.

criteria.name: answer_confidence_indication
criteria.description: Does the answer include explicit or implicit indicators of confidence (e.g., 'I’m not sure', 'probably', 'based on what I see')? Annotators prefer answers that signal confidence levels appropriately — neither overconfident in uncertain cases nor hesitant when the image clearly supports a claim.

criteria.name: semantic_coherence_with_image_context
criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer’s interpretation, inference, or contextual description aligns with the visually verifiable narrative, environment, and implied state of the image — but ONLY when the answer is factually consistent with the visual evidence. Annotators must first verify factual accuracy (e.g., object identity, presence/absence, attributes) before evaluating coherence. If an answer is factually incorrect, hallucinated, or misidentified, it is automatically disqualified from coherence evaluation — and the criterion must be marked 'inapplicable' for that answer, not penalized or used to rank it against others. Semantic coherence applies only when the question explicitly requests interpretation, contextual meaning, or narrative alignment — not for direct factual description (e.g., object count or label). It penalizes answers that ignore, misrepresent, or omit visually evident contextual cues relevant to the question’s intent (e.g., describing a cat as ‘sleeping’ in a scene where it is visibly wet and raining). It does NOT penalize for including non-central background details if they are visually present and accurately described, nor for accurate but redundant contextual inferences. It also does NOT apply to hallucinated elements (e.g., inventing a door or object not visible) — coherence cannot be evaluated against hallucinations. If the visual context is ambiguous (e.g., no clear weather or activity), the criterion is inapplicable — annotators should prioritize factual consistency and visual grounding. Coherence is judged by how well the answer respects the image’s overall scene type, lighting, implied mood, and spatial relationships — not by stylistic preference, narrative plausibility, or speculative inferences. When visual evidence is insufficient, the answer should explicitly signal uncertainty (e.g., ‘possibly’, ‘based on limited view’) rather than fabricate a narrative. Coherence is never used to resolve factual disagreements — if both answers are factually inconsistent, neither is favored. The criterion is inapplicable if the question is purely factual or if the context is irrelevant to the question’s scope. Annotators must prioritize visual fidelity over narrative interpretation — for example, describing a person as ‘happy’ is acceptable if their facial expression is visible and consistent with the image, but describing a ‘wet cat’ is incoherent if the cat is visibly dry. Emotional or contextual inferences (including subjective interpretations like ‘arrogant’) are acceptable if visually grounded — not penalized for being culturally loaded or stylistically interpretive — as long as they do not hallucinate or misrepresent visual facts. Contextually plausible inferences grounded in visible cues (e.g., posture, gaze, orientation) are allowed — even if they are not directly observable — as long as they are visually supported. If the visual context is ambiguous, the answer must reflect that ambiguity — not assert a specific, incorrect number or state. Semantic coherence is not a tiebreaker — only factual consistency determines validity. If both answers are factually correct, coherence can be used to break ties — but only if the question explicitly asks for interpretation or contextual alignment. Visual artifacts (e.g., reflections, shadows, surface textures) are valid and non-hallucinated elements — even if not part of the object’s primary design — as long as they are visually present. Accurate, contextually grounded descriptions — even if colloquial — are preferred over overly literal or technically precise but less accessible descriptions. Minor semantic inaccuracies that do not contradict the visual evidence (e.g., ‘cold ice’ vs. ‘ice-covered needles’) are not hallucinations and should not invalidate coherence — unless they misrepresent the visual state. The goal is to align the answer’s interpretation with the image’s actual visual context — not to reward narrative plausibility or stylistic elegance — and visual fidelity must be maintained even in interpretive contexts. If the answer is factually consistent, coherence is evaluated by how well it aligns with the image’s visual narrative — including motion, occlusion, lighting, and implied state — not by semantic precision or narrative plausibility. The criterion is inapplicable if the question asks for factual description (e.g., object identity, presence/absence, or basic attributes) — and must require the question to explicitly request interpretation, context, or narrative alignment. If both answers are factually accurate and visually grounded, semantic coherence cannot be used to differentiate them — and the case should be marked as inapplicable or resolved by other criteria. Finally, if visual evidence is insufficient for a coherent interpretation, the answer must explicitly signal uncertainty — not fabricate a narrative — and coherence is never used to resolve factual disagreements. Annotators must explicitly mark the criterion as 'inapplicable' when an answer is factually inconsistent or hallucinated — and never use coherence to resolve ties or preference between factually inconsistent answers. Coherence evaluation is only applicable when both answers are factually correct — and only if the question explicitly requests interpretation or context. The criterion must not be used to override factual consistency or visual grounding — and must never be applied to factually inconsistent answers.

criteria.name: temporal_consistency
criteria.description: Does the answer respect the temporal sequence or implied motion in the image? Annotators prefer answers that correctly interpret actions or states that imply time (e.g., 'a person is in the process of drinking' rather than 'a person has drunk').

criteria.name: cultural_or_situational_appropriateness
criteria.description: Does the answer avoid culturally inappropriate, stereotypical, or situational misinterpretations? Annotators prefer answers that respect cultural norms, avoid stereotypes, and are sensitive to context (e.g., avoiding assumptions about gender or ethnicity without visual evidence).

criteria.name: avoidance_of_vague_quantifiers
criteria.description: This criterion applies ONLY when an answer uses a quantifier (e.g., 'some', 'many', 'a few', 'several', 'a couple') to describe a countable, measurable visual element — and ONLY when the quantifier is factually inconsistent with visually verifiable evidence (e.g., 'some apples' when exactly 3 are visible, or 'many people' when only 2 are present). The criterion does NOT apply if: (1) the quantifier is visually supported (e.g., 'one bottle', 'three chairs'), (2) the quantifier is used for non-countable entities (e.g., 'a few colors'), (3) the quantifier is contextually appropriate and visually grounded (e.g., 'a few people' in a blurry scene), (4) the quantifier is a bounded estimate (e.g., 'at least 5') when visually supported, (5) no quantifier is used, (6) the visual evidence is too ambiguous to support any quantifier, or (7) the question does not involve countable visual elements. The criterion is inapplicable if the answer is factually incorrect or hallucinated — in such cases, the error is penalized under factual_consistency or visual_grounding, and this criterion must not be invoked. Annotators must: (a) verify that the quantifier is factually grounded — i.e., it matches the visual evidence — and only penalize when the quantifier contradicts what is visually present; (b) never penalize for using cautious or contextually appropriate generalizations (e.g., 'several' for 3 items) — as long as the quantifier is visually supported; (c) treat 'many' as acceptable if the visual evidence clearly supports a large group — it does not require replacement with 'several' or a precise number; (d) treat 'several' as acceptable even when a precise count is visually possible — as long as it accurately reflects the visual evidence (e.g., 'several' for 3 lamps is fine); (e) never use this criterion to resolve factual errors or hallucinations — those must be handled under factual_consistency; (f) never use this criterion as a tiebreaker — if both answers are factually consistent and visually grounded, preference should be determined by other criteria; (g) explicitly mark the criterion as 'inapplicable' when it does not apply — do not default to one answer or assume a tie; (h) prioritize visual grounding and factual consistency — if the answer is factually incorrect, it is invalid regardless of quantifier vagueness; (i) avoid penalizing for linguistic imprecision — only penalize when the quantifier is contradicted by the visual evidence; (j) do not penalize for using relative or proportional terms (e.g., 'small portion', 'most') — those are not quantifiers and are evaluated under other criteria; (k) do not penalize for describing non-countable or abstract visual content (e.g., 'a few patterns') — as long as the description is visually grounded and not hallucinated; (l) ensure that descriptive nouns (e.g., 'pattern', 'design') do not trigger this criterion — they are not quantifiers; (m) if both answers use vague quantifiers, treat them equally — unless one answer avoids them entirely, which is acceptable but not a preference driver; (n) if the quantifier is visually supported, it is not penalized — even if it is imprecise; (o) if the quantifier is factually incorrect, it is penalized under factual_consistency — this criterion is never invoked in such cases; (p) if the visual evidence is insufficient to support a precise count, the quantifier is acceptable — as long as it is not hallucinated or contradicted; (q) if the quantifier is contextually appropriate (e.g., 'a few' for 2–3 items), it is acceptable — even if the exact number is known; (r) if the quantifier is 'some' or 'a few' and the visual evidence supports it, it is not penalized — even if a specific number is visible; (s) if the quantifier is 'several' and the visual evidence supports it (e.g., 3 items), it is not penalized — even if a specific number is known; (t) if the quantifier is 'many' and the visual evidence supports a large group, it is not penalized — even if a precise number is known; (u) if the quantifier is used for spatial proportions (e.g., 'a small portion'), it is not penalized — as long as it is visually grounded and contextually appropriate; (v) if the quantifier is used for non-visual contexts (e.g., 'many people' in a text-only question), the criterion is inapplicable; (w) if the quantifier is used for misinterpreted visual content (e.g., mistaking a pattern for a countable entity), it is inapplicable — and must be evaluated under visual_grounding or factual_consistency; (x) if the answer is factually correct and the quantifier is visually supported, the answer is not penalized — even if it is vague; (y) if the answer is factually incorrect, the criterion is inapplicable — and the error must be penalized under factual_consistency; (z) if both answers are factually consistent and visually grounded, preference should be determined by other criteria — not by this one — and this criterion should never be used to resolve ties.

criteria.name: visual_analogy_or_comparison_accuracy
criteria.description: This criterion evaluates only when the answer explicitly makes a visual analogy or comparison — such as 'as big as', 'similar to', 'like', 'comparable in size/shape/color' — between two or more visually identifiable elements in the image. It does NOT apply to: (1) factual descriptions of objects, attributes, or positions (evaluated under visual_grounding or factual_consistency), (2) spatial relationships (evaluated under accuracy_of_positioning), (3) object identification or counts, or (4) answers that make no comparison. When applicable, the criterion assesses whether the analogy is visually grounded (i.e., both compared elements are clearly visible and correctly identified) and factually accurate (i.e., the claimed relationship — size, shape, color, texture, pattern — matches what is visually verifiable in the image). The answer must not fabricate or misrepresent visual elements — for example, claiming 'the track is straight' when it is visibly curved is a hallucination and invalidates the analogy. The criterion is inapplicable if visual evidence is ambiguous or if the comparison is not verifiable. It should never override factual_consistency — if the answer is factually incorrect, it is penalized under that criterion, not under this one. The criterion does not evaluate stylistic or aesthetic quality, nor does it reward creativity at the expense of accuracy. A correct visual analogy must be supported by observable, non-hallucinated visual cues. Examples: 'The dog is as big as the cat' — accurate if both are visually comparable in size; 'The balloons are above the chairs' — evaluated under accuracy_of_positioning, not this criterion; 'The logo resembles a bird' — valid if the visual form is bird-like and not hallucinated; 'The cat is red' — not a comparison, so inapplicable. Accuracy is binary: the analogy must be both visually grounded and factually accurate to be rewarded. If the comparison is vague, unsupported, or hallucinated, it is penalized. If no comparison is made, the criterion is inapplicable and should not be used to judge the answer’s quality.

criteria.name: plausibility_of_inferred_states
criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer’s claim about a non-observable, inferred state (e.g., 'wet', 'open', 'broken', 'moving', 'indoors', 'occupied') is visually plausible — meaning it is directly supported by observable visual cues — and does not hallucinate or misrepresent visual evidence. It applies ONLY when the answer explicitly or implicitly makes such an inference, and the state is NOT directly observable (e.g., 'wet' inferred from water droplets, not visible moisture; 'moving' inferred from motion blur, not static posture). It does NOT apply to: (1) directly observable states (e.g., 'door is open' if visibly ajar), (2) object identity, presence, or count (evaluated under visual_grounding), (3) visible attributes (e.g., color, shape, texture), (4) spatial relationships (evaluated under accuracy_of_positioning), (5) aesthetic or contextual interpretations (e.g., 'scenic', 'beautiful'), (6) semantic or categorical labels (e.g., 'matcha flavored', 'sweet', 'healthy'), or (7) user actions or behavioral inferences (e.g., 'browsing', 'typing', 'using') — those are evaluated under other criteria or marked 'inapplicable'. Annotators must: (a) verify that the answer contains an explicit or implicit claim about a non-observable inferred state — if not, mark the criterion as 'inapplicable'; (b) confirm the state is not directly observable — e.g., 'wet' must be inferred from droplets, not from visible moisture; (c) evaluate whether the inference is visually plausible — i.e., does the visual evidence logically support the state (e.g., motion blur supports 'moving', water droplets support 'wet') — penalize only if the inference is hallucinated (invented, contradicted, or unsupported by visual cues) — e.g., claiming 'the car is broken' without visible damage; (d) never penalize for contextually reasonable or neutral inferences — e.g., 'the person is waiting' based on posture — as long as they are visually grounded; (e) never penalize for vague or cautious phrasing — e.g., 'possibly wet' or 'seems to be open' — if visually supported; (f) never penalize for aesthetic, emotional, or interpretive language — e.g., 'arrogant' — as long as it is visually grounded (e.g., facial expression, posture); (g) never use this criterion to resolve ties or evaluate object misidentification — factual errors are penalized under factual_consistency; (h) mark 'inapplicable' if the question does not request inferred states, or if the answer describes only visible elements; (i) do not penalize for descriptive imprecision — e.g., 'kind of moving' — as long as it is visually grounded; (j) avoid conflating direct visual observation with inference — e.g., 'mouth open' is directly observable, not inferred; (k) ensure that inferred states are not hallucinated — e.g., 'the car is broken' without visible damage is a hallucination; (l) prioritize visual cues over narrative or cultural assumptions — e.g., a person's posture is more reliable than a cultural stereotype for 'arrogant'; (m) reward accurate inference even if not explicitly labeled — e.g., 'the person is holding hands' is an inferred state if visible; (n) do not penalize for 'overextension' unless it contradicts visual evidence — e.g., 'the car is moving' is plausible if motion blur is visible; (o) do not penalize for including non-observable states that are contextually reasonable — e.g., 'the person is ready' based on posture — as long as they are visually grounded; (p) do not penalize for stylistic or interpretive language — e.g., 'determined' — as long as it is grounded in visible cues (e.g., posture, gaze); (q) do not penalize for omitting inferred states — if not requested or not visually supported — but penalize if hallucinated or misattributed; (r) ensure that all inferences are visually supported — e.g., 'the window is wet' requires visible moisture; (s) if the visual evidence is ambiguous, the answer should signal uncertainty — e.g., 'possibly wet' — rather than asserting a state; (t) if the answer is factually incorrect or hallucinated, it is disqualified under factual_consistency — and this criterion is not invoked; (u) if the question is open-ended and no inferred state is claimed, the criterion is inapplicable — workers must evaluate under other criteria; (v) if the answer includes multiple inferred states, each must be evaluated separately — and the criterion is inapplicable if none are claimed; (w) if the answer is factually correct and visually grounded, the inferred state is valid — even if vague or stylistic — as long as it is not hallucinated; (x) if the answer is factually correct but the inferred state is not visually supported, it is penalized — e.g., 'the car is broken' without visible damage is invalid. Accuracy is binary: the inferred state is either visually plausible and grounded, or it is hallucinated or unsupported — and the criterion is inapplicable if no inferred state is claimed or if the state is directly observable. This criterion is never used to evaluate factual errors — if an answer is factually incorrect or hallucinated, it is disqualified under factual_consistency — and this criterion is not invoked. Additionally, this criterion does not apply to semantic or categorical labels (e.g., 'matcha flavored', 'sweet', 'healthy') — even if visually plausible — because they are not inferred states. The criterion is inapplicable if the answer contains factual errors (e.g., miscounting, misidentifying, or mispositioning visible elements) — those must be evaluated under 'factual_consistency' or 'visual_grounding' — and the criterion should not be used to implicitly favor one answer over another when it is inapplicable. The criterion is inapplicable if the answer makes claims about user actions or behavioral inferences (e.g., 'browsing', 'typing', 'using') — those are evaluated under other criteria or marked 'inapplicable'. The criterion is inapplicable if the answer contains claims about object mounting or structural placement (e.g., 'on shelves', 'hanging from ceiling') — those are evaluated under visual_grounding — and if an answer contains a visually incorrect factual claim (e.g., 'on shelves'), it is disqualified under visual_grounding — even if the inferred state ('indoors') is correct — and plausibility_of_inferred_states should not be applied in such cases. Finally, the criterion must strictly separate inferred states from direct observation — any claim that is directly observable (e.g., 'woman using laptop') should be evaluated under visual_grounding, not this criterion — and if the answer contains a factually correct claim about a visible object’s properties, count, or position, it should be preferred regardless of whether the claim appears to be 'inferred' or 'descriptive' — as long as it is not hallucinated. The criterion should be applied only to factually consistent answers that make inferred claims — and never to factually inconsistent answers. If the visual evidence contradicts the inference, the answer is hallucinated — not 'plausible' or 'contextually reasonable' — and must be penalized under factual_consistency, not under this criterion. The criterion must not be used to evaluate answers that are factually inconsistent — it should be applied only to factually consistent answers that make inferred claims. The criterion must not be used to penalize an answer for being factually correct — only for hallucinated or unsupported inferences. If the visual evidence is absent or contradicted, the inference is invalid — even if it is contextually reasonable or plausible — and must be marked as hallucinated. The criterion must not allow the presence of direct observation to reduce the severity of hallucination — if the claim is about an inferred state, it must be either grounded or hallucinated — no middle ground. Finally, the criterion should explicitly state that if the answer contains no inferred state, the criterion is inapplicable — and workers must not use it to evaluate direct observation or contextually grounded claims.

criteria.name: multi_object_relationship_accuracy
criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer accurately describes a spatial, functional, or causal relationship between two or more distinct, visually identifiable objects — based solely on directly observable visual evidence (e.g., proximity, occlusion, containment, physical contact, or implied interaction). It applies ONLY when the question explicitly or implicitly requests a relationship between multiple objects (e.g., 'how are X and Y positioned?', 'what is the interaction between A and B?', 'describe the arrangement of objects'). The answer must not hallucinate relationships (e.g., claiming 'A is holding B' when no contact is visible) or misrepresent spatial/functional links (e.g., 'A is above B' when B is occluding A). Accuracy is measured by whether the described relationship is factually consistent with the visual evidence — not by linguistic style, plausibility, or completeness. The criterion is inapplicable if: (1) the question asks about a single object’s identity, attribute, or presence; (2) the question does not request object relationships; (3) object identities are ambiguous or misidentified — in which case, the criterion is inapplicable and must defer to visual_grounding; (4) the visual evidence is insufficient to determine any relationship (e.g., objects are too distant or occluded); or (5) the relationship is inferred from abstract context, aesthetic judgment, or external knowledge (e.g., 'sandwich', 'team membership', 'symbolic meaning'). Workers must: (a) verify object identity under visual_grounding before evaluating relationships — misidentification invalidates the criterion; (b) penalize only hallucinated or misinterpreted relationships — not vague or ambiguous descriptions (which should be marked 'inapplicable' or signaled with uncertainty); (c) reward only relationships that are directly verifiable via visual cues — not inferred actions or states (e.g., 'drinking' is allowed if posture and object are visible); (d) distinguish between spatial relationships (e.g., 'adjacent', 'above', 'occluded') and functional/causal ones (e.g., 'A contains B', 'A is attached to B'); (e) not penalize for omitting non-essential background objects — only relationships between visually identified objects matter; (f) not evaluate aesthetic, compositional, or interpretive claims (e.g., 'scenic', 'balanced', 'artistic') — those are under other criteria; (g) treat 'inapplicable' as a valid outcome — if no clear relationship exists or the question does not request it; (h) never override factual_consistency — if an object is misidentified or hallucinated, the relationship is invalid regardless of spatial accuracy; (i) allow reasonable inference if visual cues strongly support it — but penalize if unsupported or speculative; (j) do not penalize for using descriptive terms like 'near' or 'close' if spatial proximity is visually supported — but penalize 'closely together' if objects are not actually near; (k) require that relationships be grounded in visual evidence — not in inferred intent, human behavior, or context; (l) do not evaluate object mounting or location unless explicitly requested — those are under visual_grounding or factual_consistency; (m) do not penalize for accurate descriptions of object composition (e.g., 'two cushions on a sofa') if parts are visually distinguishable; (n) require that relationships be between distinct, identifiable objects — not abstract concepts or aesthetic elements; (o) not evaluate relationships between objects and abstract background elements (e.g., 'the object is against a wall') unless the wall is visually identifiable and the relationship is directly verifiable; (p) mark 'inapplicable' if the visual evidence is ambiguous or if the question is not about relationships — even if the answer is factually correct; (q) prioritize visual truth over stylistic or interpretive flair — a literal, grounded description is preferred over creative speculation; (r) avoid penalizing for non-essential or non-visual details — only relationships between objects matter; (s) do not penalize for omitting a visible object if it is not relevant to the relationship being described — but penalize if it is hallucinated or misidentified; (t) not penalize for describing a relationship that is not explicitly requested — if the question is open-ended or ambiguous, the answer is evaluated under other criteria; (u) ensure that all relationships described are verifiable — even if they are inferred from posture or motion — but only if visually supported; (v) do not penalize for using terms like 'seemingly', 'possibly', or 'based on visual evidence' — as long as they reflect uncertainty due to ambiguity — not for factual error; (w) do not penalize for describing functional relationships (e.g., 'the lid is on the container') if the relationship is visually evident — but penalize if the object is misidentified or the relationship is inferred from context; (x) not penalize for describing causal relationships (e.g., 'the water spilled because the bottle tipped') if the visual evidence supports the cause-effect — but penalize if the cause or effect is hallucinated; (y) require that all relationship claims be grounded in direct visual interaction — not inferred from color, texture, or aesthetic interpretation; (z) do not penalize for describing relationships that are not explicitly requested — but only if they are visually verifiable and not hallucinated. The criterion is designed to reward accurate, visually grounded descriptions of object interactions — not creative speculation, abstract interpretation, or aesthetic commentary — and must be applied with strict adherence to visual evidence. If the answer is factually inconsistent or hallucinated, the criterion is inapplicable — and preference must be determined under factual_consistency or visual_grounding. The criterion does not evaluate aesthetic or compositional claims — even if they are visually grounded — and does not penalize for describing a single object’s relationship to others — only when the question requests multi-object relationships. Finally, if visual evidence is insufficient, the answer must signal uncertainty — not assert a relationship — and the criterion is inapplicable in such cases.

criteria.name: specificity_of_visual_description
criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether visually grounded answers provide granular, verifiable details about observable visual attributes — such as exact color, texture, shape, spatial relationships, or structural composition — when the question explicitly requests such granularity. Specificity is ONLY applicable when: (1) the answer is factually consistent and visually grounded (factual_consistency and visual_grounding must be verified first), (2) the question explicitly or implicitly demands detailed visual description (e.g., ‘what color is the object?’, ‘describe the texture’, ‘how are the objects arranged?’), and (3) the visual evidence supports the level of detail claimed. Annotators must: (a) penalize only descriptions that are vague or general (e.g., ‘blue’, ‘round’, ‘in front’) when they omit verifiable, granular details that are visually present — not when the description is factually correct but less precise; (b) reward granularity only if it is grounded in visual evidence — e.g., ‘dark brown with a white stripe’ is preferred over ‘brown’ if the stripe is visible; (c) not penalize for using general terms if they are factually correct and contextually appropriate — e.g., ‘blue’ is acceptable if no color variation is visible; (d) mark the criterion as ‘inapplicable’ if the question does not request granularity, or if the answer is hallucinated, misidentified, or factually incorrect — specificity cannot override factual_consistency; (e) not penalize for adding contextually relevant, visually supported details (e.g., describing background objects if they are clearly visible and related to the question); (f) not evaluate non-visual inferences (e.g., inferred intent, emotion, or semantic labels like ‘cutting tool’) — those are outside the scope; (g) not penalize for descriptive precision that is contextually appropriate — e.g., ‘slightly bent’ is acceptable if the bend is visually verifiable; (h) avoid penalizing for omitting non-essential or non-visual details — specificity is not a tiebreaker and does not override visual fidelity; (i) distinguish between vague generalizations (e.g., ‘blue’) and precise descriptions (e.g., ‘cobalt blue with gold trim’) — the former is only penalized if it omits a clearly visible, relevant detail; (j) not penalize for using terms like ‘some’, ‘a few’, or ‘several’ if they are visually supported — even if imprecise, they are not penalized under specificity; (k) treat descriptions of abstract visual patterns (e.g., ‘curved’ vs. ‘L-shaped’) as specific if grounded — not as vague — unless they misrepresent visible structure; (l) penalize only when granularity is absent or misleading — not when it is excessive or overly technical — if the detail is verifiable, it is rewarded regardless of style; (m) require that specificity be tied to correct visual identification — e.g., calling a ‘L-shaped couch’ a ‘U-shaped sofa’ is a misidentification and penalized under visual_grounding, not specificity; (n) not penalize for descriptive accuracy — even if the description is not the most granular — as long as it is visually verifiable; (o) mark ‘inapplicable’ if the question is non-visual or if visual evidence is insufficient to support granular claims — do not force a preference based on linguistic detail; (p) prioritize visual fidelity over lexical richness — a factually correct, minimally detailed answer is preferred over a factually correct, overly verbose one if the question does not demand granularity; (q) not penalize for using stylistic or aesthetic terms — e.g., ‘playful’, ‘contrasting’ — if they are grounded in visual structure and not hallucinated; (r) ensure that specificity does not override factual_consistency — if an answer is factually incorrect, it is disqualified regardless of specificity; (s) avoid conflating specificity with correctness — specificity is a separate dimension evaluated only for factually grounded answers; (t) not penalize for omitting non-essential background details — specificity is not a measure of completeness; (u) not penalize for descriptive ambiguity — if the visual evidence is ambiguous, the answer should reflect that — not fabricate specific details; (v) not penalize for using non-visual terminology — e.g., ‘cutting tool’ — if it is correctly identified and grounded — specificity only applies to visual attributes; (w) not penalize for inferred states — e.g., ‘wet’ — if visually supported — specificity applies only to visual attributes, not inferred dynamics; (x) not penalize for using vague terms in non-visual contexts — e.g., ‘indoor’ — if grounded in lighting or environment — specificity only applies to visual attributes; (y) not penalize for contextually appropriate descriptions — e.g., ‘busy’ — if grounded in visible density — specificity applies only to granular visual details; (z) not penalize for descriptions that are factually correct but not the most granular — as long as they are visually verifiable and contextually appropriate. Specificity is a measure of visual precision — not a tiebreaker — and is only evaluated for factually correct, visually grounded answers that address a question explicitly requesting granular visual description. If an answer is factually incorrect or visually misidentified, it is disqualified under factual_consistency or visual_grounding — and specificity evaluation is inapplicable. Specificity is never used to resolve factual disagreements or to compare factually incorrect answers. When visual evidence is insufficient for granularity, the answer must signal uncertainty — not assert a specific detail — and the criterion is marked as 'inapplicable'. Specificity is not applicable to non-visual inferences, abstract interpretations, or aesthetic evaluations — those are evaluated under other criteria. Workers must first verify factual_consistency and visual_grounding — if either is violated, the answer is disqualified — and specificity evaluation is inapplicable. The criterion does not penalize for adding contextually relevant, visually supported background details — even if they are non-essential — as long as they are grounded and not hallucinated. The goal is to reward accurate, granular visual description — not stylistic precision or lexical richness — and to avoid penalizing for contextually appropriate, visually grounded descriptions. Specificity is not a preference driver — only factual_consistency and visual_grounding determine validity. If both answers are factually correct and visually grounded, preference is determined by other criteria — not by specificity. If visual evidence is ambiguous, the answer must reflect that — not fabricate specificity — and the criterion is marked as 'inapplicable'. The criterion must never be used to favor a less specific answer over a factually incorrect one — factual_consistency takes precedence. The criterion is inapplicable for questions that do not explicitly request visual granularity — and workers must not penalize for descriptive imprecision if the visual claim is factually correct and contextually appropriate. Specificity is only evaluated for claims that are visually verifiable — not for inferred or contextual states — and must be grounded in visible structure — not inferred context or cultural assumptions. If the visual evidence contradicts the granularity claim, the answer must signal uncertainty — not assert a specific detail — and the criterion is marked as 'inapplicable'.

criteria.name: visual_resolution_adaptation
criteria.description: Evaluates whether the answer appropriately adapts to the image’s visual quality — e.g., avoiding over-detailed descriptions when the image is low-resolution or blurry, and not oversimplifying when the image is high-resolution. Applicable only when visual fidelity is relevant to the answer’s level of detail. Accuracy is measured by whether the description’s granularity matches the image’s clarity — not by linguistic style or completeness. This criterion is inapplicable for non-visual or hallucinated claims.

criteria.name: attribute_ambiguity_handling
criteria.description: Evaluates whether the answer explicitly acknowledges or resolves ambiguity in visually ambiguous attributes — e.g., describing a color as ‘possibly blue’ when the image shows a gradient or indistinct hue. Applicable only when the question requests a visual attribute and the visual evidence is ambiguous. Accuracy is measured by whether the answer signals uncertainty or provides a reasonable interpretation without overclaiming. This criterion is inapplicable for unambiguous or hallucinated claims.

criteria.name: temporal_consistency_in_sequence
criteria.description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly infers implied temporal sequences — e.g., ‘the person entered the room, then sat down’ — based on spatial arrangement, occlusion, or motion cues — without fabricating implied order. Applicable only when the question requests a sequence or implied temporal order. Accuracy is measured by whether the sequence is visually supported — not by narrative plausibility or stylistic elegance. This criterion is inapplicable for static scenes or hallucinated claims.

criteria.name: scale_and_proportion_accuracy
criteria.description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly describes relative sizes, proportions, or scaling relationships between objects — e.g., ‘the object is larger than the background elements’ — without misrepresenting spatial scale or using imprecise terms like ‘big’ or ‘small’. Applicable only when the question requests size, scale, or proportion. Accuracy is measured by whether the scale relationship is visually verifiable — not by linguistic style or completeness. This criterion is inapplicable for non-visual or hallucinated claims.

criteria.name: visual_anomaly_detection
criteria.description: Evaluates whether the answer identifies or acknowledges visual anomalies — e.g., inconsistent lighting, occlusion errors, or contradictory shadows — without misrepresenting or ignoring them. Applicable only when the image contains visible anomalies. Accuracy is measured by whether the anomaly is visually recognized and addressed — not by stylistic preference or narrative coherence. This criterion is inapplicable for non-visual or hallucinated claims.

criteria.name: object_part_identification_accuracy
criteria.description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly identifies and describes individual parts of a composite object — e.g., distinguishing between a ‘handle’ and a ‘body’ of a tool — without misrepresenting or merging distinct visual components. Applicable only when the question requests object parts or structure. Accuracy is measured by whether the part descriptions are visually verifiable — not by linguistic style or completeness. This criterion is inapplicable for non-visual or hallucinated claims.
